rich_summary: This section continues the tale of the churning of the Ocean of Milk. As the gods and Asuras churn Mount Mandara, the process devastates sea creatures and forests while fire and storms erupt around the mountain. The gods grow exhausted and appeal to Brahma, who asks Narayana (Vishnu) to restore their strength so the churning can continue. One by one the ocean yields its treasures: the Moon, Lakshmi, the divine horse, the Kaustubha gem, and finally Dhanvantari carrying the vessel of amrita. The Asuras claim the nectar, but Vishnu uses illusion, taking the form of an enchanting woman to seize it. When the gods drink the nectar, the disguised Asura Rahu attempts to share it; Vishnu beheads him, explaining the mythic origin of eclipses. The deception triggers open war between gods and Asuras.

highlight_spans.why: The violent cosmic imagery of the churning—storms, fire, and devastation—sets the mythic scale of the event.
The gods, exhausted and unable to continue, appeal to Brahma and Narayana—marking the turning point that allows the churning to resume.
The emergence of divine treasures from the ocean—Moon, Lakshmi, the celestial horse, and the Kaustubha gem—forms the central payoff of the churning myth.
Siva swallows the deadly Kalakuta poison to save creation, a dramatic act of cosmic sacrifice explaining his epithet Nilakantha (blue‑throated).
Rahu secretly drinks the nectar but is exposed by Surya and Soma; Vishnu decapitates him, establishing the mythological cause of eclipses.

top_scenes.scene_text: Mount Mandara whirls in the ocean as storms, lightning clouds, and fire erupt while crushed sea creatures and uprooted forests swirl in the churning waters.
Dhanvantari rises from the ocean holding the white vessel of amrita as gods and Asuras stare in awe and greed.
Vishnu’s discus slices off Rahu’s head as he drinks the nectar among the gods, the severed head rising toward the sky while the body crashes to earth.
